definition: A group of cells with a similar structure and function working together.
A group of different tissues working together to perform a specific function.
A group of organs working together to perform a major function in the body.
The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
A biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions without being used up.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself.
The specific region on an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
The molecule that fits into the active site of an enzyme and is broken down.
The model describing how a specific substrate fits into the specific active site of an enzyme.
When an enzyme's active site changes shape permanently due to high temperature or extreme pH, so the substrate no longer fits.
The pH at which an enzyme works at its fastest rate.
The temperature at which an enzyme works at its fastest rate.
An enzyme that breaks down starch into sugars. Produced in the salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.
An alkaline substance produced by the liver, stored in the gall bladder, that emulsifies fats and neutralises stomach acid.
The process by which bile breaks large fat droplets into smaller droplets, increasing surface area for lipase to work.
Tiny finger-like projections lining the small intestine that increase surface area for absorption of digested food.
The wave-like muscular contractions that push food along the digestive system.
Glands in the mouth that produce saliva containing amylase to begin the digestion of starch.
A muscular organ that produces protease enzymes and hydrochloric acid to digest proteins and kill bacteria.
The organ where most digestion and absorption of nutrients takes place.
The organ where water is absorbed from undigested food, forming faeces.
A gland that produces digestive enzymes (amylase, protease, lipase) and releases them into the small intestine.
An organ that produces bile, processes nutrients, removes toxins and stores glycogen.
A muscular organ that pumps blood around the body, consisting of four chambers.
One of the two upper chambers of the heart that receive blood coming in from the body or lungs.
One of the two lower chambers of the heart that pump blood out to the lungs or body.
A structure in the heart or veins that prevents the backflow of blood.
A blood vessel that supplies the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart, with thick muscular walls and no valves.
A blood vessel that carries blood towards the heart, with thin walls and valves to prevent backflow.
The smallest blood vessel, one cell thick, where exchange of substances between blood and tissues occurs.
A metal mesh tube inserted into a blocked coronary artery to keep it open and restore blood flow.
Drugs used to lower blood cholesterol levels and reduce the risk of coronary heart disease.
The force exerted by blood against the walls of the blood vessels, measured in mmHg.
The pale yellow liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances including nutrients, hormones and waste products.
A blood cell containing haemoglobin that carries oxygen around the body. Has no nucleus and a biconcave shape.
A blood cell that is part of the immune system, defending against infection by engulfing pathogens or producing antibodies.
A small fragment of a cell in the blood that helps blood to clot at a wound.
The red pigment in red blood cells that binds to oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.
A condition where the coronary arteries become narrowed by a build-up of fatty deposits (plaques), restricting blood flow to the heart.
A fatty deposit that builds up inside artery walls, narrowing the lumen and restricting blood flow.
A disease caused by uncontrolled cell division, forming a tumour that can invade other tissues.
A growth of abnormal cells that remains in one place and does not spread to other parts of the body.
A cancerous tumour that can invade neighbouring tissues and spread to other parts of the body via the bloodstream (metastasis).
The spread of cancer cells from the original tumour to other parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system.
The region of plant tissue where cell division occurs, found at the tips of roots and shoots.
Plant tissue made of dead hollow cells that transports water and mineral ions from roots to leaves.
Plant tissue made of living cells that transports dissolved sugars from leaves to the rest of the plant.
The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant through the stomata.
Tiny pores on the surface of leaves that allow gas exchange and water vapour to escape.
Cells surrounding stomata that control their opening and closing by changing shape when they gain or lose water.
The transport of dissolved sugars and other substances through the phloem from leaves to other parts of the plant.
The outer layer of cells covering plant organs, providing protection.
A layer of cells just below the upper epidermis of a leaf, packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
